item.title: bicep-deploy vs bicep-action: A Tool or a Workflow?
item.description:
Azure/bicep-deploy vs bicep-action: A Tool or a Workflow?

I maintain innofactororg/bicep-action, so I should say up front that I am not a neutral party. I am also the person who most needs this comparison to be honest, because every time someone evaluates bicep-action for a new estate, the first question is the obvious one: why not just use Microsoft’s?

item.title: bicep-action: Plan, Review and Deploy Bicep from Pull Requests
item.description: Terraform teams stopped deploying blind years ago. They open a pull request, a bot runs terraform plan and posts the result as a comment, a colleague reads exactly what will be created, changed and destroyed, and only then does anyone type atlantis apply. Most Bicep teams still merge and find out. The pipeline runs, the deployment succeeds or fails, and the first time anyone sees what Azure actually did is in the activity log afterwards.

item.title: Azure Quota Groups: Recycling Capacity You Already Own
item.description: The most expensive vCPU in Azure is the one you already had approved, gave back by accident, and now have to ask for again. That is exactly what happens every time an old subscription is cancelled. Years of quota increases, each one a support ticket, a business justification and a few days of waiting, disappear with the subscription. Meanwhile the brand-new subscription that replaces it starts life with default limits, in a region where capacity is tight, and the first deployment into it fails with a quota error the platform team then has to chase.

item.title: From Azure DevOps Wiki to a Corporate PDF
item.description:
The project documentation is in good shape. The team has been maintaining an Azure DevOps wiki, the architecture pages link to the detailed design, and the deployment instructions sit alongside the decisions that explain them.

Then comes the handover request: “Can you send us the design document as a PDF? Please use the company template.”

That is a reasonable request. The recipient might not have access to Azure DevOps. An architecture board may need a fixed version to review, or the customer may need to file the document in a records system. A wiki is useful for the people doing the work; a controlled document is useful for the people accepting it.

item.title: Running Tailscale on a Ubiquiti EdgeRouter
item.description:
Having grown up in the world of ‘on premise’ computing, I have always prioritized data privacy in my home network.

Though there may not be much of interest to hackers, there is still personal data and services that I want to keep secure. I have spent years working with OpenVPN and IPSec, building and supporting a Dynamic Multi-site VPN Mesh with Cisco DMVPN, and I know first hand the challenges of connecting clients to a private network and managing keys.

item.title: Considering Terraform and Bicep
item.description:
As more organizations adopt cloud infrastructure, the demand for infrastructure as code (IAC) solutions has grown. Infrastructure as code allows developers to manage and automate infrastructure deployments using code, making it easier to track changes and maintain consistency.

Terraform and Bicep are two popular IAC solutions that enable developers to manage and automate infrastructure deployments using code.

While both tools share some similarities, Terraform is more widely adopted solution with many benefits, In this post, we will highligh some of the benfits each expose, so you can start to figure out where you next learning should be focused

item.title: Theming Hugo with Module
item.description:
To utilize modules in Hugo for our theme, we first must ensure that our site supports Hugo Modules.

You can quickly verify that you site is configured for Hugo Modules, as it should contain a go.mod file in the repository root.

Import the theme module

The concept of a Hugo theme has been superseded with the concept of modules, with the main difference that the former will allow you to build your site entirely, while the latter might implement only some modular features like enabling the ATOM feed, or adding a search to your website.

item.title: Change Detection using Oxidized
item.description:
The process is very simple:

  1. Login to each device in the router list router.db,
  2. Run Commands to get the information that will be saved
  3. Clean the output
  4. Commit the Changes to GIT Repository

The tool is coded in Ruby, and implements a Domain Specific Language (DSL) for interaction.

Finally, there is a Web based User experience included in the solution so we can get a fast overview of the world.

item.title: Azure Functions Scaffolding
item.description:
Most of my time is spent working on Governance in Azure; and while the cloud native plumbing is amzaing, there are still some gaps which need to be filled, and my go-to tool of choice is Azure Functions.

One of the products which I oversee the devleopment of is called the ‘Concierge’ and recently maintaining it has been a challange instead of a joy. It was architected with Fuctions v1 principals, and its well time for a look inside the tool box.

item.title: Azure IaC - Function Keys
item.description:
Todays conundrum: As I deploy a new Function Application, I need a simple methodology to retrieve the Host Keys for the function application so that I validate the deployment has been successful; and potentially pass on the key to related services, for example API Management.

As before, I am leveraging templates, and will stay cloud native; this time depending on the functions Output ability to present the keys.
